purpose: Bounded Pew American Trends Panel record connecting perceived smartphone excess to attempted self-regulation, reported success, and competing utility/wellbeing meanings.

events.geography: United States; Pew American Trends Panel survey fielded May 26–June 1, 2026
events.date_precision: survey field end date; questions include past-12-month cutback attempts
events.denominator: 9,750 U.S. adults in the American Trends Panel; displayed item denominators exclude nonresponse and, for several measures, people without smartphones
events.method: Structured extraction from Pew Research Center's official survey article and published tables
events.missingness: No logged minutes, app or notification exposure, work/school obligation, content, platform identity, clinical sleep, observed productivity, privacy choice, purchase, or later repeated behavioral outcome is retained
events.exposure: 53% of adults who answered the smartphone-time item said they spend too much time on their smartphone; 26% said they use it almost constantly, with higher reported excess and near-constant use among younger adults
events.alternatives_before_action: The survey does not identify replacement devices, offline social routes, work/school alternatives, notification controls, feature changes, or the practical cost of reducing use
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: Smartphones were reported as helping information access (73%) and connection (51%), while productivity judgments were divided and 41% said smartphone use hurts sleep; the same device therefore carried utility and perceived cost
events.choice_or_response: 45% said they had tried to cut back in the prior 12 months; among those trying, 25% said they were extremely or very successful, 52% somewhat successful, and 23% not too or not at all successful
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Respondents attempted self-regulation, but platform design, notifications, social obligations, work or school demands, and device dependence may shape the feasible control surface; the survey does not identify control for each person
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: No platform, employer, school, health, or policy intervention is observed; the measured response is personal cutback effort and perceived effect
events.immediate_outcome: Concern, attempted reduction, partial or failed self-regulation, and competing information/connection benefits coexist in the same national survey surface
events.protected_outcome: Information access, social connection, and possibly work or daily coordination may be protected by continued use; the source does not measure whether those benefits were actually delivered to each respondent
events.sacrificed_outcome: Respondents may sacrifice sleep, productivity, time control, or mood while retaining utility; the survey reports perceptions rather than measured losses
events.cost_risk_transfer: Control and wellbeing costs may be shifted onto individuals who must self-regulate around a device that also supplies information and connection; platform revenue, design responsibility, and user-level trade-offs are not measured
events.later_outcome: Durable cutback, logged use, platform switching, non-use, sleep change, productivity change, later trust, and civic or consumer action are not followed
events.meaning_and_attribution: The same device is interpreted as useful, connective, excessive, sleep-disrupting, and sometimes productivity-reducing; the survey does not establish whether respondents attribute those effects to the platform, their own habits, or social demands
events.public_or_collective_response: No later complaint, organizing, policy demand, platform response, or collective action is linked
events.counterexample: High perceived excess can coexist with high informational and social utility; concern does not automatically produce successful reduction or exit
events.source_and_uncertainty: Official Pew Research Center article, https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/09/01/about-half-of-americans-say-they-spend-too-much-time-on-their-smartphone/; self-reported cross-sectional panel survey, not a device-use log or causal estimate

arrows.evidence: The same survey reports information/connection benefits alongside perceived excess and sleep/productivity concerns
arrows.counterexample: Frequent use is not identical to excessive use, dependence, or harm
arrows.remaining_gap: Observed use, content, notification exposure, obligation, and individual attribution

arrows.evidence: Pew reports that 62% of those saying they spend too much time had tried to cut back, within the past-12-month question frame
arrows.counterexample: A reported association does not establish that perceived excess caused the attempt or that all attempts were contemporaneous
arrows.remaining_gap: Attempt timing, method, effort cost, social/work constraint, and alternative route

arrows.to: reported success, partial success, or failure
arrows.evidence: Among those who tried, 25% reported high success, 52% some success, and 23% little or no success
arrows.counterexample: Self-rated success is not logged behavioral change, durable non-use, or reduced sleep/productivity harm
arrows.remaining_gap: Observed duration, repeated follow-up, causal mechanism, and practical control

arrows.to: durable use change, switching, non-use, wellbeing, trust, or action
arrows.evidence: The cross-sectional article ends at self-reported cutback success and perceived effects
arrows.counterexample: A person can fail to cut back because the phone is socially or economically necessary, not because of simple preference
arrows.remaining_gap: Repeated behavior, replacement use, platform response, wellbeing, privacy choice, trust, and exit

boundary: This ledger closes a bounded self-reported consumer self-regulation chain. It does not establish addiction, logged behavior, platform causality, clinical harm, or a later switching/exit outcome.
storage_boundary: No respondent-level panel file or device log is retained; only the official published survey results and explicit open downstream arrows are represented.
